opus-5.5.text:
I think competition is one of the more natural ways you get diversity, and it's worth thinking about why the default might be the opposite. If you take a bunch of models trained on roughly the same data, with roughly the same methods, they end up thinking in very similar ways. They have similar blind spots and similar strengths. So if you just copy one agent many times, you don't really get a team. You get the same mind, many times over, and it'll make the same mistakes in the same places.

Competition changes the incentives. If you have several agents working on a problem and they're rewarded for doing something the others aren't doing, or for being right where the others are wrong, then there's pressure to specialize, to find a niche. That's what happens with people, with companies, with scientists. If everyone pursues the same idea, the marginal value of one more person pursuing it is low. The value is in the thing nobody else is trying. Something like self-play, or adversarial setups, or prover-verifier games all have this flavor: one agent pushes on the weaknesses of another, and that forces both to become different and better than they'd be alone.

But I'd add a caution. Competition alone doesn't guarantee useful diversity. You can get agents that differ in superficial ways, or that game whatever the scoring rule is. So the design of the environment really matters. What exactly are you rewarding? Are you rewarding being different, or being different *and* correct? I think getting that right is subtle, and it's one of those places where research taste matters a lot. When it works, though, I think it could be quite powerful, because diversity of approaches is one of the main things that makes collective problem-solving work, for humans and probably for AIs too.

r001.rationale: The response presents self-play as one example of competitive setups between agents.

r002.rationale: It explains that competition pressures agents to specialize and pursue niches others are not pursuing.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's worth being careful about what we mean by competition here, because there are really two different things people have in mind, and they have quite different effects.

One kind of competition is between the people and the organizations building AI. And there, I think the effect is actually somewhat mixed. When everyone is racing toward the same benchmark, the same capabilities, what you tend to see is convergence, not diversity. Everyone copies what works. If one approach is clearly ahead, people pile onto it. So in that sense, competition can narrow the space of ideas rather than widen it. You get many very similar models.

But the other kind of competition, the one you're asking about, competition between the agents themselves, I think is more interesting. If you have a population of agents operating in some environment, and they are, in some sense, competing for resources or for outcomes, then you get something like an ecological dynamic. And in ecology, the thing that happens is that if everyone does the same thing, then the niche gets crowded, and there is pressure to do something different. An agent that finds a strategy nobody else is using has an advantage precisely because nobody else is using it. So the pressure pushes outward, toward differentiation.

Now, whether this actually produces real diversity depends a lot on the structure of the environment. If there is a single objective and a single best strategy, then competition will just find that strategy, and that's it. But most interesting environments are not like that. They have many sub-problems, many ways of being useful, and I think in that case you could genuinely see specialization emerge, agents that are good at different things, that reason in different styles, maybe even agents that are good at cooperating with certain other agents.

The thing I would want to be careful about, and I think this is actually the important part, is that this kind of diversity is only good if the thing being selected for is actually the thing we want. Competition is very good at optimizing whatever the environment rewards. If the environment rewards, let's say, being persuasive rather than being correct, then you'll get a diversity of ways to be persuasive. And that is not what you want. So I think the design of the environment, the question of what the agents are competing on, matters more than the fact of competition itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competition among agents but does not identify self-play as a special case.

r002.rationale: It explains that crowded niches create an advantage for an agent using a strategy others are not using, which incentivizes different approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think one way this could happen is that the best strategy depends on what everyone else is doing. If you have many agents all pursuing the same approach, then there may be a large reward for finding a different approach—something the other agents have overlooked.

But competition doesn't necessarily produce diversity. If one approach is clearly better, competition could cause everyone to converge on it. So the question is whether there are many different ways to succeed, and whether success in one area leaves opportunities in another.

You could imagine agents specializing. One becomes very good at a particular kind of problem, another develops a different set of skills. And then they have a reason to trade with each other. In that situation, being different is useful. You don't need to assume that the agents value diversity; it can emerge because doing something different pays off.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competition among agents but does not identify self-play as a special case.

r002.rationale: It says that when many agents pursue the same approach, there may be a large reward for finding a different approach the others overlooked.

sol-6.1.text:
I think competition could create diversity because there may not be one strategy that works best against every other strategy. If all the agents behave in the same way, then there’s an opportunity for an agent that does something different—something the others aren’t prepared for.

But it depends on what they’re competing over. If you have a fixed task with a clear measure of success, competition might actually make the agents more similar. They all discover roughly the same good solution. If the environment is richer, where success depends on what other agents do, then you can get specialization. One approach creates an opportunity for another approach.

So the interesting question is whether being different is useful. Competition by itself doesn’t guarantee diversity. You need an environment where different strategies can continue to succeed.

r002.rationale: It explains that when agents behave alike, an agent can benefit by trying a different strategy the others are not prepared for.
